title: How Disgust Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore disgust as a subject of scientific study: its origins in distaste and evolutionary psychology, Paul Rozin's categories (core, animal-nature, moral), the gape facial expression, the pre-germ-theory aversion to corpses, the moral-disgust brain research, political exploitation of disgust, cultural variation, disgust sensitivity and phobias, and the disgust scale quiz. The episode ends with a listener mail about dyslexia.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to disgust research
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the topic, note that science hasn't fully explained disgust, and discuss Paul Rozin as a founder of the field and his claim that disgust separates humans from other animals. They note the field only took off in the 1970s and 1990s and mention early thinkers Darwin and Sangiel.

segments.title: Three categories of disgust
segments.summary: Rozin's categories are described: core disgust (contaminants like vomit and feces), animal-nature disgust (reminders of being animals, such as eating with hands, poor hygiene, bodily violation), and moral disgust. The universal gape facial expression is discussed with skepticism.

segments.title: Evolutionary origins: distaste and Tuk and Mock Mock
segments.summary: Disgust is theorized to have grown out of the involuntary distaste reflex that spits out bitter or rotten food. A hypothetical story of two hunters illustrates natural selection, with the alternative idea that the lesson was passed on as a meme. The hosts discuss the imagination-based step that lets people feel disgust without eating.

segments.title: Disgust toward corpses and pre-germ-theory origins
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why dead bodies disgust people, noting a 2004 Biology Letters study finding potential disease-threat images rated as more disgusting. They question where the idea of disease transference from corpses came from before germ theory, which is about 150 years old, and consider the role of competing contingencies such as hunger versus disgust.

segments.title: Moral disgust, brain imaging, and political exploitation
segments.summary: Brain research shows the anterior insula lights up both for disgusting objects and for unfair treatment in the ultimatum game. Haidt, Rozin and McCauley's work finds cross-language use of disgust for moral offenses, and that disgust-sensitive people lean socially conservative, which the hosts say media imagery can exploit.

segments.title: Break and bathroom humor
segments.summary: A break with informal banter about flatulence studies and an anecdote about a stranger asking about farting at a concert.

segments.title: Recap, cultural variation, and disgust phobia
segments.summary: The hosts recap the evolutionary path from distaste to moral disgust, then discuss cultural variation in what is disgusting (food, taboos), how tastes can be learned or changed (veganism, broccoli, texture), and how excessive disgust can become compulsive cleanliness or phobia, referencing the film Safe.

segments.title: Disgust triggers: acne, slugs, and the disgust scale quiz
segments.summary: Acne and slugs and snails are cited as triggers because they resemble disease or mucus. The hosts take sample items from the disgust scale, including questions about a jar with a preserved hand, toilet seats, urine, and intestines, and reflect on fainting at visceral sights.

segments.title: Listener mail on dyslexia
segments.summary: Listener Audrey Short shares her experience with dyslexia, attending the Shanks School and using Orton-Gillingham, graduating with a biochemistry and physics degree from Miami University of Ohio, and encouraging others with learning disabilities to seek help.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and point them to the website and email address.
